REUTERS/Anatolii Stepanov By Olena Harmash and Yurii Kovalenko KYIV, Aug 1 (Reuters) - Russia pounded Kyiv and the region in a heavy ballistic missile attack early on Saturday, killing 10 people, as President Volodymyr Zelenskiy warned that Ukraine had run out of interceptor missiles for ‌its U.S. Patriot air defence systems. Zelenskiy said that Russia launched 35 missiles at Ukraine, including 27 ballistic missiles, and also 185 drones. ‌Only one ballistic missile was intercepted, "simply because there are no interceptors for the Patriot system", he said. Advertisement Advertisement More than a dozen explosions reverberated through the city during several waves of attacks, ​according to Reuters witnesses. "Every package of ballistic missile interceptors saves the lives of our people. And every night without them results in more casualties," Zelenskiy said on the Telegram app. With the war in its fifth year, fighting is raging along about 1,200 kilometres (750 miles) of front line. But Russian advances have slowed by more than half this year, and Ukraine has been launching strikes inside Russia hitting its oil facilities, logistics sites and weapons production. Ukraine was bringing back ‌war to Russia, Zelenskiy said, adding that his troops ⁠struck the infrastructure of three oil refineries in the Bashkortostan region and other targets that sustained Moscow's war effort. Advertisement Advertisement Russia has also intensified its attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities. Ukraine relies on U.S.-made Patriot air defence systems, ⁠but the Iran war has seen supplies of interceptor missiles previously earmarked for Ukraine diverted to the U.S. military and U.S. allies in the Gulf. Moscow and Kyiv both deny targeting civilians in the war launched by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. SECOND MAJOR ATTACK ON KYIV THIS WEEK Saturday's is the second major ​attack on ​Kyiv this week after nine people, including six members of one family in ​a village near Kryvyi Rih, were killed on Thursday and ‌a suspected Russian cruise missile landed in Poland. Advertisement Advertisement Damage was recorded in seven districts across Kyiv, a city of about 3 million people, the Prosecutor's General Office said after Saturday's attacks. Zelenskiy said that fires broke out across Kyiv and 18 residential buildings, a school, the Lithuanian Embassy, and infrastructure facilities were damaged. Ukrainian prosecutors said seven people were killed in the Darnytskyi district on the left bank of the Dnipro river and two more people died in the Solomyanskyi district on the right bank of the city. One more person was killed in the Kyiv region where the attacks damaged several warehouses, ‌regional officials said. Advertisement Advertisement Dozens of people in Kyiv and the region were injured, including four ​children who suffered multiple shrapnel wounds and lacerations. "I looked at my phone, it was 1:30 (22:30 ​GMT) and sirens (blared), I was lying dressed in my bed, I ​got up immediately. And at once explosions started - boom, boom," said Nadiia Komarova, a 68-year-old concierge at an apartment ‌building in Kyiv. "Our ceilings have started to crumble. My window ​here is smashed, and everything has fallen ​inside," she told Reuters. Reuters television footage showed police and rescuers working on the site. Two rescuers put a body in a black sack in a car. Firefighters were extinguishing fires and charred cars stood near an apartment building. Advertisement Advertisement Mayor Vitali Klitschko said Kyiv was working ​to build and prepare more shelters as attacks continue ‌to intensify. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha issued a fresh plea for urgent air defence supplies. "It is the battle for the skies that ​will define the trajectory of this war. The stronger the air shield over Ukraine, the closer peace becomes." Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Tilda Swinton in Man to Man at the Royal Court in 2026. Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The Guardian Theatre ‘Female survival in a terrifying world’: Tilda Swinton’s return in Man to Man Manfred Karge’s play about a woman acting as her dead husband was a cause célèbre in the 80s. It remains a bracing portrait of a divided person in a divided culture Stephen Unwin Thu 10 Sep 2026 05.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google It was Pierre Audi, the much-mourned founder of the Almeida , who way back in 1986 sent me a coffee-stained copy of Jacke wie Hose. Manfred Karge ’s one-woman play is a study of female survival in a terrifying world. Ella is a working-class woman who takes on the identity of her dead husband, Max, to endure what Brecht memorably dubbed “the dark times”: the 12 years of Nazi rule. But Karge extends this to include the division of Germany into two nation states (one communist, one capitalist) and the reconstruction that followed. My German was just about good enough to realise that this was something that had to be seen, and soon Jenny Killick, the visionary artistic director of the Traverse in Edinburgh, commissioned a translation from Anthony Vivis and had the guts to give the go-ahead for what we called Man to Man. Tilda Swinton and I were close friends from Cambridge, and we’d often worked together, at university and in the real world. She was the obvious choice to play the part. View image in fullscreen Surprising and challenging … Tilda Swinton in Man to Man at the Royal Court in 1988. Photograph: Donald Cooper/Alamy Along with the designer Bunny Christie and the lighting designer Ben Ormerod, we soon had a team, all in our 20s, all just starting out, all making it up as we went along. But our scratch production became a cause célèbre at the 1987 Edinburgh festival, and transferred to the Royal Court for a three-week run the following year. In a theatre culture devoted to poetic naturalism, it surprised and challenged audiences. And it shaped us all. Even then, Manfred Karge was a legendary figure. He was born in poverty in Brandenburg before the war, and his talent was spotted in 1961 by the great Helene Weigel – Bertolt Brecht’s wife, who had co-founded the Berliner Ensemble after the war and ran it following his death. She quickly engaged Karge as an actor. He also became a director, working in many of the leading German-speaking theatres. He wrote Jacke wie Hose, his first play, which he staged with his partner, Lore Brunner, in Bochum in 1982. He returned to Berlin in 1993, where he still writes, directs and teaches. Karge is one of the last surviving links to the original Brecht theatre. And in true Brechtian spirit, he wrote a deliberately conflicted figure: likeable one moment, repellent the next; insightful and blinkered; reactionary and visionary; but, throughout, a woman from the lowest rung of society, caught up in the disastrous contradictions of her time. Thus, Man to Man shows a divided person in a divided culture in a divided land. It explores the deepest forms of alienation – social and political, sexual and psychological – in which identities are fluid and, as Marx said, all that is solid melts into air. And in Karge’s two new scenes (one written specifically for this revival), we see the fall of the Berlin Wall and the re-emergence of the German far right, and how these divisions continue to multiply. View image in fullscreen A woman caught up in the disastrous contradictions of her time … Tilda Swinton in Man To Man in 2026. Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The Guardian Man to Man is an extraordinary text. Its 28 short scenes deploy a heady cocktail of verse and prose, doggerel and naturalistic chatter, as well as fragments of songs, poems and quotations from both “high” and “low” culture. It is idiomatic and peculiarly hard to translate. The title literally means “jacket like trousers”, the equivalent, perhaps, of “six of one, half-a-dozen of the other”. We’re delighted to be returning to the late Anthony Vivis ’s stunning English version, to which I’ve made some minor revisions and added translations of the two new scenes. Karge’s text provides no stage directions, no sense of how he wants it to be presented, and every creative team must come up with their own answers. Revisiting the play after all these years, Tilda, Bunny, Ben and I are eager to do two things at once: celebrate what worked in our original production while testing those responses against new realities, new ways of making theatre. Happily, we’re joined by younger collaborators, ready to challenge us, primed to contribute, and determined to make this much more than a revival from the distant past. Tilda Swinton’s blast from the past, Kevin Bridges at large and a deepfake ballet: theatre, comedy and dance to see this autumn Read more Sometimes, we’ve found, history overtakes us. Thus, in 1987 I suggested to Bunny that a thin line of red tape bisecting the white floor could suggest the division of Germany and the Berlin Wall, which I had recently crossed. And now, nearly 40 years later, we are confronted with a new scene in which the Wall comes tumbling down: Tilda ripping up that red tape from the floor will be one of those rare moments when the practical nature of the theatre will act out history itself. The theatre must live in the present tense. But it also has a past and a future. The wheel has come full circle. We are here. Man to Man is at the Royal Court theatre, London , until 24 October. Then at the Traverse theatre, Edinburgh , 29 October to 7 November, and in New York in February. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/29/new-.text: Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed a decree to boost the army by 15,500 troops in the fourth such order this year."The authorised ... strength of the Russian armed forces is to be set at 2,441,630 units, including 1,550,500 military personnel," the decree said.Putin previously signed decrees boosting the army's size in March, June and July. The combined increase since March amounts to 47,860 soldiers.Russia's president did not state the reason for the decision, but it has been taken against the backdrop of rising losses in Moscow's full-scale war in Ukraine.This year, Russian advances on the battlefield have slowed, as widespread drone use has made rapid movement of large troop units almost impossible. In recent weeks, reports have also emerged of Ukrainian breakthroughs on certain sections of the front.The last time Putin announced a "partial mobilisation" of reservists was in September 2022 after a series of setbacks at the front. That decree remains in force.Signs of a new mobilisation?In August, Ukraine's intelligence services reported that Moscow plans to call up up to 300,000 people this year for deployment to the front, and the same number again next year.A number of analysts, citing data on preparatory measures by Russian authorities on the ground, predicted a new wave of mobilisation as soon as this autumn, immediately after elections to the State Duma, triggering renewed fears among ordinary Russians of being dragged to the front and a surge of interest in emigration.Putin dismissed these rumours as "utter nonsense". The Kremlin insisted that contract soldiers and volunteers were meeting the needs of Russia's armed forces, while independent analysts say recruitment among them continues to shrink despite promises of large financial rewards."In essence, Russia has already begun additional mobilisation, it is expanding the scale of recruitment to its ranks, using various methods for this," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday, commenting on Putin's decree in a video address published on X."It also plans to increase the number of foreigners, and it is important that the governments of the countries from which Russia recruits people into its ranks counteract this," he added.Zelenskyy said that he has new data indicating that North Korea is preparing to send 10,000 of its soldiers to Russia, in addition to the 8,000 who have already been deployed there.

https://www.politico.eu/article/trump-sa.text: President Donald Trump said Monday he was open to a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, but said such a meeting would not focus on the war in Ukraine. Trump told reporters at the White House that he would participate in a summit with both leaders if the purpose was to discuss denuclearization. The comments came after reports that Putin had proposed that the three leaders meet on the sidelines of next month’s APEC summit in China to discuss how to end the war in Ukraine. “I would do it, not so much for Ukraine,” Trump said. “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They have not been doing much. And the same thing with China. We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons, denuclearization. And anytime I can have a meeting on denuclearization.” Advertisement Advertisement Trump made room for the possibility of other topics to be discussed in such a meeting but reiterated that it would be “based on denuclearization.” “If President Xi wants to have it, I’d have it,” he said. “I’m sure we would talk about other things like trade too but yeah I would do that.” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov confirmed to The Wall Street Journal that discussions were taking place over the possibility of a meeting, but there was no “clear understanding” yet about what the potential summit’s agenda would consist of. The possibility of a high-level summit between the three leaders comes as Trump has waived sanctions on Russia and announced a diesel deal with Putin , while placing the blame for the four-year war on Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who earlier Monday briefed a bipartisan group of lawmakers about the conflict . “To be honest, I think it is time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine, because what has happened?” Trump said to reporters. “Very little land has moved, but a million people, a tremendous number of people are dead.”

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvx2.text: Image source, Getty Images By Aleks Phillips Published 25 October 2026, 08:15 GMT Updated 1 hour ago Elon Musk has said his company SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink internet service, after Ukrainian officials said connectivity issues appeared to have been resolved. The tech billionaire accused Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using it for military activity - but denied being responsible for a simultaneous issue with its US-run, military-grade counterpart Starshield. Kyiv has not officially commented on Musk's latest claim but Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said his post was "very strange". Musk had earlier denied deliberately throttling Ukraine's connection, which it says hampered its ability to conduct defensive operations for more than a week. The issue first emerged last week during a broader row between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure. Musk's latest comments, and the seeming restoration of the service, came after US President Donald Trump said he had told the Tesla and X owner to "put it back", having repeatedly denied instructing him to limit the service. "Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote on X on Saturday. "Ukraine['s] military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week." He went on to say that SpaceX had "done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth" and reiterated his stipulation that Starshield was a different system and controlled by the US government, adding: "What they decide to do is up to them." He added in a later post: "[Starlink] can be used for infrastructure that is military, but it cannot be used for unequivocally offensive strikes that make it fair game to be struck back." Reacting to Musk's post, Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram that Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine have a speed restriction of 70-90km/h and do not work on Russian territory. "Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and medium-range strikes," he said. "It is very strange that Elon Musk is not aware of Starlink restrictions in Ukraine." There was no immediate comment from Ukraine's defence ministry. Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed, both of which run on networks of low Earth orbit satellites launched by SpaceX. Starlink allows military units to co-ordinate, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield, while Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones. Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work. Ukraine's Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said earlier on Saturday that the military was now recording a "stable connection", with drones now able to reach speeds in excess of 400km/h (249mph). Kyiv previously said the connection would cut out above 161km/h. "The speeds are now where they need to be," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram. Musk did not disclose in his post why SpaceX had chosen to make the change to its service last week, when Ukraine's extensive use of Starlink had been known for several years. The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic standoff between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia. Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher. While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war . Faced with midterm elections next month and domestic displeasure with rising fuel prices, Trump waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal with Moscow - criticised by European allies as funding Russia's war machine - to supply Russian diesel to the US and the global market. Zelensky initially agreed to do so on the proviso that Russia cease striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, before restarting the strikes after several instances of Moscow disregarding this. The Ukrainian leader said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied. Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap? Published 4 hours ago Fighting and aerial attacks continue to be exchanged between Russia and Ukraine overnight. Ukraine's emergency services said three people were killed and 15 others injured, including an 11-year-old girl, in attacks on the Dnipropetrovsk region, in the south east. Another six people were injured when a Russian drone struck an apartment block in the central city of Vinnytsia, it said. The Russian defence ministry said on Sunday that it had struck a cargo vessel it claimed was being used to supply the Ukrainian army while it was en route to the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk overnight. It also said Russian forces hit a logistics centre, a distribution centre and a logistics terminal in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv. Ukraine's defence ministry earlier said it struck a facility in the Russian city of Oryol run by a sanctioned heavy machinery manufacturer. Russian authorities said three people were killed in the strike.
